newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia hails Deng Xiaoping as great reformer.
newsitem.headline: Australia hails Deng Xiaoping as great reformer.

text.p: Australia on Thursday paid tribute to Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping, who died on Wednesday, hailing him as a great economic reformer.

"Undeniably his economic leadership was so strong and it greatly helped revamp and modernise the Chinese economy, that those directions are now irreversible," Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer told Australian Broadcasting Corp radio.
Fischer, who is also Trade Minister, said Deng's death would not affect Sino-Australian relations.
The office of Prime Minister John Howard, due to visit Beijing next mnonth, had no immediate comment.
However, Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said Australia was not concerned about a leadership struggle in Beijing.
"We don't see any immediate changes in China," Downer said in a radio interview from the Papua New Guinea capital, Port Moresby, where he is on an official visit.

"The Chinese leadership have been making preparations for his death for a long time and in recent times the Chinese leaders have really reaffirmed the economic path that Deng had laid out, so we wouldn't expect any immediate changes," he said.

"Deng was very much the architect of modern China, he opened up the Chinese economy and he really ended the economic harshness which was above all demonstrated by the cultural revolution," Downer said.
He said any political reform was unlikely in the short term.
"The broader question about political reform is one that is frankly rather a long way down the track," he said.

"The present leadership -- the younger ones and the older ones -- are very committed to the existing political structure as well as, though, importantly, to the process of economic reform and I don't see any change to that in the immediate future at all," Downer said.
Fischer said Deng's economic reforms had benefited the Asia-Pacific region and China had lost a historic figure.

"There's plenty of evidence that he was a big catalyst to the U-turn, effectively, which China made over recent decades to liberalising the economy, opening up the economy, making wealth creation a legitimate aim for the people of China at all levels, and that was pretty radical stuff," Fischer said.

"We owe a great deal to Deng Xiaoping because of course the knock-on of that (economic reform) has reached far beyond China and contributed to economic growth right across this part of the world," Fischer said.
"I express my condolences to the president and people of China -- they have lost a person who made a very real historic contribution to the economic development of China."
Downer said Australia's economic relationship remained strong, after political "ups and downs" in 1996 over a range of security and diplomatic issues.
"In recent months ... the relationship has been moving ahead very well politically," he said.
Deng died of respiratory failure while in the advanced stages of Parkinson's disease on Wednesday night.
